issues.description: Collapsing working and walking conflates two distinct DFS phases the data model used to separate.
issues.detail: The old state machine had unsorted -> working (children pushed) -> walking (cycle-detection during descent) -> sorted. Merging working and walking into one label means push() can no longer distinguish 'currently descending' from 'children queued but not yet entered'. If the cycle-detection in push relied on that distinction, this is a behavioral change disguised as a cleanup. The data shape changed; verify the algorithm still follows.

issues.description: clear(s.stack) before reslicing to zero length is redundant work.
issues.detail: clear() zeroes every element of the backing array, then s.stack = s.stack[:0] drops the length. Either the clear is for GC of pointer elements (fine, say so) or it's superstition. For a stack of Node values that may hold pointers, zeroing is right; for value types it's wasted. One line of intent beats two lines of ceremony.

issues.description: Cleanup-on-defer changes the lifetime contract of Sorter state without documenting it.
issues.detail: Previously state was cleared on next Sort() entry; now it's cleared on iterator completion. That's the better choice (memory released sooner, reuse is cheaper) but it's a contract change worth a one-line comment on the Sorter struct so the next reader doesn't 'optimize' it back.

issues.description: Updated comment contains typos: 'visisted' and 'if its'.
issues.detail: Small thing, but the comment is the load-bearing explanation of why each node is visited twice. 'visisted' -> 'visited', 'if its' -> 'if it's'. Comments that explain the algorithm deserve the same care as the code.

issues.description: Yield-failure path now leaves state[k] unset, which matters if the caller restarts.
issues.detail: Previously s.state[k] = sorted ran unconditionally after pop. Now it only runs when yield returns true. Since the defer clears state anyway this is fine for the current API, but it couples correctness to the defer in a way the prior code did not. Worth a comment that early-return relies on the defer wiping state.

review.summary: TOO-CLEVER on the state-collapse, SMALL-AND-COMPOSABLE on the cleanup move. Merging 'working' into 'walking' is a real data-structure change, not a rename — the two labels encoded different DFS phases, and push() reads that label. Verify the cycle-handling branch still behaves the same with one label doing two jobs; if it does, the simpler state is a win, but the PR description undersells it as a cleanup. Defer-based teardown is the right call. Fix the comment typos while you're in there.
